title: Maresius: threefold faith-act — disposing, formally justifying, consoling
source_text: LXV. His plane gemina docet Samuel Maresius, in Systemate, loco undecimo, Thesi 57. Triplex, inquit, fidei actus venit in justificatione consideratione & distinguendus: Unus dispositivus, quo credo Christum suis meruisse remissionem peccatorum, juxta doctrinam Evangelii, adeoque & mihi remissum iri mea peccata, si resipuero, & vera fide acquieuero in merito Christi. Et cum hunc fidei actum comitentur miseriae nostrae ex Dei lege agnitio, & illa fames & sitis justitiae, de quibus Matth. 5. vers. 6. his simul reus ponitur in statu, ut loquuntur Pragmatici, sententiae sibi absolutorium consequendae & audiendae. Quare ut fides quoad hunc actum praeit actualem remissionem peccatorum in foro poli & conscientiae, ita etiam praescribitur in Verbo ad illam obtinendam. Secundus justificatorius formaliter, quo mihi per Spiritum adoptionis ipsa justificatoria & absolutorium sententia pronunciatur & intimatur: credo in praesens mihi hic peccato dolenti, & serium emendationis studium deinceps posidenti, Deo per Christum esse remissa omnia mea peccata, tum ea quae hactenus commisi, tum ea in quae possum labi deinceps per infirmitatem; & Deum illa nunquam mihi imputaturum ad condemnationem, sed ex imputata Servatoris mei justitia me pro innocente habiturum, & certo donaturum vita aeterna. Atque hic actus simul est tempore cum actuali justificatione & remissione peccatorum. Tertius consolatorius, quo in praeterito credo fuisse jam mihi remissa omnia mea peccata, & me nulli amplius subesse condemnationi, ut loquitur Paulus, Rom. 8. vers. 1. atque confido illam sententiam absolutorium mihi antea intimatam, extensum & applicatum iri Dei misericordia ad peccata quotidianae incursiones, quorum etiam quotidie to sensu remissionem peto in Oratione Dominica. Et hic fidei actus justificationem & remissionem peccatorum subsequitur. Unde liquet quo sensu & quousque fides sit conditio ad salutem perquisita; nam primo sensu fides se habet ad justificationem antecedenter, secundo simultanee, tertio consequenter.
pass_a_gloss: To these Samuel Maresius teaches things plainly twin, in his System, locus eleven, Thesis 57. A threefold act of faith, he says, comes to be considered and distinguished in justification: One disposing, by which I believe that Christ has merited for his own the remission of sins, according to the doctrine of the Gospel, and so that my sins also will be remitted to me, if I repent and with true faith rest in the merit of Christ. And since this act of faith is accompanied by the acknowledgment of our misery from God's law, and that hunger and thirst for righteousness of which Matthew 5:6 speaks, by these together the guilty person is placed in the state, as the Pragmatists speak, of a sentence of absolution to be obtained and heard. Wherefore as faith in respect of this act precedes the actual remission of sins in the forum of heaven and of conscience, so also it is prescribed in the Word for obtaining that remission. The second is formally justificatory, by which through the Spirit of adoption the very justificatory and absolving sentence is pronounced and intimated to me: I believe that in the present, to me here grieving for sin and thereafter possessing a serious zeal for amendment, all my sins are remitted by God through Christ — both those I have hitherto committed and those into which I may afterward fall through weakness; and that God will never impute them to me unto condemnation, but from the imputed righteousness of my Savior will hold me for innocent, and will certainly give me eternal life. And this act is simultaneous in time with actual justification and remission of sins. The third is consolatory, by which in the past I believe that all my sins have already been remitted to me, and that I am no longer under any condemnation, as Paul speaks, Romans 8:1; and I trust that that absolving sentence formerly intimated to me will be extended and applied by God's mercy to the sins of daily encroachment, whose remission I also daily seek with earnest sense in the Lord's Prayer. And this act of faith follows justification and the remission of sins. Whence it is clear in what sense and how far faith is a condition required for salvation; for in the first sense faith stands to justification antecedently, in the second simultaneously, in the third consequently.
pass_b_english: Maresius (System, locus 11, Th. 57): a threefold act of faith must be marked in justification.

Disposing act: I believe Christ has merited remission for his own, and that my sins will be remitted if I repent and rest in his merit — with law-bred misery and the hunger of Matt. 5:6 setting the guilty under an absolving sentence yet to be heard.

Formally justificatory act: by the Spirit of adoption the absolving sentence is spoken into me now — present remission of past and future weakness-sins, never imputed to condemnation, innocence from Christ's imputed righteousness, and certain eternal life; simultaneous with actual justification.

Consolatory act: past-tense confidence that all sins were already remitted and condemnation is gone (Rom. 8:1), with trust that absolution stretches to daily falls sought in the Lord's Prayer — this follows justification.
So faith is saving condition three ways: before, with, and after justification.
